source.title_on_document: Effects of Varying LLM Access on Essay Writing Behavior

supplement.where: No external supplement is mentioned. Appendix A (study procedure, consent form, condition instructions, limited-group system prompt, pre- and post-surveys, grading rubric) is inside this PDF, pp. 12-17.

paper_design_summary: 24 undergraduate and graduate students at the University of Minnesota were randomly placed into three groups (control with no LLM, limited LLM access with at most 3 prompts and responses under 100 words, unlimited LLM access) and wrote a short argumentative essay of about 300 words in an individual in-person session of about 30 minutes. Two writing-center consultants graded the essays on a seven-item rubric, and the authors computed Root type-token ratio and the cosine similarity between each essay and that participant's LLM responses. A post-session survey asked about ownership, perceived creative expression, and originality.

studies.label: Pilot study: essay writing with no, limited, or unlimited LLM access

assignment.what_was_assigned: Level of LLM access while writing the essay: none (control), limited (Gemini-2.5-Flash chatbot with a restrictive system prompt, at most 3 prompts, responses under 100 words), or unlimited (same chatbot, no prompt limit or special instructions).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly placed into one of three groups: control, limited access to LLM, or unlimited access.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 3.2 (Study Procedure); also p. 1, Abstract

arms.name: Control
arms.description: No LLM help; AI writing browser extensions disabled.

arms.name: Limited LLM
arms.description: Gemini-2.5-Flash chatbot with a system prompt restricting it to general guidance, responses under 100 words, at most 3 prompts.

arms.name: Unlimited LLM
arms.description: Same Gemini-2.5-Flash chatbot with no prompt limit, no restricted token output, and no special instructions; participants were told not to ask it to write the full response.

participants.who: Undergraduate and graduate students with 18 different majors at the University of Minnesota - Twin Cities, recruited by email; eligibility required native-level English fluency (Table 1, N = 24). Per-arm count of 8 comes from the Figure 5 caption (p. 6) and matches the Figure 3 histograms.
participants.quote: We recruited a total of 24 undergraduate and graduate students with 18 different majors through email recruitment.
participants.locator: p. 2, Section 3.1; p. 3, Table 1 (N=24); p. 6, Figure 5 caption (8 participants per group); p. 1, Abstract

ai_tool.name_model: Gemini-2.5-Flash, through a custom chatbot web app (Flask and Python, deployed on Vercel)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants in the two LLM arms chatted with the bot through a provided link while writing in Google Docs. The limited arm had at most 3 prompts and a system prompt telling the model to give short general guidance and not write paragraphs; the unlimited arm had no limit. Both arms were told not to have the AI write the full response.

task.description: Argumentative opinion essay on whether college students should pursue subjects that interest them rather than courses most likely to lead to jobs. The main methods request at least 300 words (p. 3, Section 3.2); condition instructions say around 300 words and at least 3 paragraphs (pp. 12-13, Appendix A.1.2). Essays were graded for writing quality using a rubric that includes originality and depth of ideas within the Ideas, Support, & Development (Evidence) criterion (p. 17, Appendix A, score-5 anchor). No separate overall-creativity score is reported.

outcomes.name: Idea Support / Ideas, Support, & Development (Evidence): mixed originality, support, and development rubric score
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two university writing consultants independently scored the essays, and their grades were averaged (pp. 4-5, Section 4.2). The rubric uses a 1-5 scale (p. 16, Essay Grading Rubric). Its score-5 anchor explicitly requires originality and depth of ideas, alongside evidence supporting the main points (p. 17, Ideas, Support, & Development (Evidence)). Coded novelty for the explicit originality component, but the score mixes originality, support, and development; it does not isolate originality or provide a standalone overall-creativity rating. AI was available during composition in the LLM arms; the Control arm had none (p. 3, Section 3.2). Only arm means are printed, without any of the complete uncertainty/statistic formats listed under statistics_available.

contrasts.reported: Table 4, average Idea Support scores: Control 4.6, Limited 4.5, Unlimited 4.7, on a 1-5 rubric. Descriptive arm means only; no category-specific SD, confidence interval, test statistic, or p-value is printed. Section 5.3 states that no significant group differences were found in grading outcomes.

outcomes.name: Final essay word count
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Final word count of each essay, recorded as output length and productivity (p. 5, Section 4.2, Writing Time and Volume). Table 5 reports average words per essay for each arm (p. 8). The paper does not specify the word-count procedure. No codebook measure category exactly covers a plain word count, so measure is null; no creativity-scoring model or lexical-overlap procedure is claimed for this outcome. AI was available during composition in the LLM arms; the Control arm had none (p. 3, Section 3.2). Only arm means are printed, without any of the complete uncertainty/statistic formats listed under statistics_available.

eligibility.reason: One individually randomized lab experiment analyzed 24 people across three arms (8 per arm; p. 1, Abstract; p. 3, Section 3.2; p. 6, Figure 5 caption). Criterion 1 is met, but criterion 2 fails because fewer than 50 people were analyzed. Criterion 3 is met: two university writing consultants scored the essays using a rubric whose Ideas, Support, & Development (Evidence) category explicitly rewards originality and depth of ideas (pp. 4-5, Section 4.2; p. 17, Appendix A, score-5 anchor; p. 8, Table 4). This is a mixed originality/support/development score, with no separate overall-creativity scale. Core remains no and context_class remains none: the study belongs in the screening report as a small randomized experiment. Root TTR measures within-essay vocabulary, and cosine similarity compares each essay with that participant's own LLM responses, so neither measures diversity across people (p. 5, Section 4.2). Reduced creative expression is self-reported (p. 15, Post-Interaction Survey, Q.7).

one_line_finding: In a 24-student pilot (8 per arm), rubric essay grades were similar under no, limited, and unlimited LLM access (88.66%, 88.39%, 89.38%; Table 4, p. 8), and unlimited-access essays were more similar to the LLM's responses than limited-access essays (cosine 0.552 vs. 0.444, ANOVA p = 0.21; Table 5 and Section 5.3, p. 8).
